parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones an animal rescue centre to ask about volunteering.
script: Good afternoon, Larkspur Animal Rescue, Tom speaking.
Oh, hello. My name's Ellen. I saw a poster in the library saying that you need volunteers, and I wondered if I could find out a bit more.
Of course, we're always glad of help. Let me just bring the volunteer form up on my screen so I can fill it in as we talk. Can I take your surname first?
Pemberton, thanks. And a contact number?
07845 221 960. Lovely. Now, have you worked with animals before, Ellen?

Well, not in a job. But I grew up with pets, we had about six rabbits at one point, and I spent a couple of summers helping out at a riding stable, although that was mostly horses and I'm not sure it counts.
It counts, but to be honest the rabbits are more useful to us. We've got a lot of them at the moment, and people forget how much care they need. So I'll put rabbits down as your main experience.
That's fine. Oh, and I'd like to do a Tuesday, if that's possible. I'm at the gym on Wednesdays.
Ah, Tuesdays are full, I'm afraid. So are Wednesdays, as it happens. Thursdays are the quietest day, and we could really do with somebody there.
Thursday's fine, then. I can rearrange things.

Great. Now, the start time depends on which team you join. The dog kennels start at 9, but we're short of people in the cat house, and the cat house starts at 9.30, because the staff feed the cats first. Would you be happy with the cats?
Oh, I love cats. Yes, please. So that's half past nine, and I finish when?

At 1.30. It's a four-hour shift, including a break. Now, before you start, everyone has to come to an induction session. It's normally held in the main office, but the office is being repainted this month, so for now we're using the barn. You'll see it behind the car park.
The barn, right. Do I need to bring anything?
Yes, some photo ID, so that we can make you a volunteer badge. A passport is ideal, but a driving licence will do. You don't need proof of your address, that's only for the paid staff.
Good, I've got my driving licence. Can I ask, is it a problem that I've only just moved to Hartwell? I don't really know anyone here yet.
Not at all. A lot of our volunteers started that way, and they've made good friends. What made you decide to come to us, if you don't mind my asking?

Well, meeting people is one reason, I suppose, and I'm thinking about vet nursing one day, though I haven't decided. But really, the main thing is that I miss having animals around. My landlord doesn't allow pets in the flat, so this is the best way I can think of to spend time with them.

That's a good reason, and honestly it's the one that keeps people coming. Now, there is a commitment. We used to ask for six months, but it was putting people off, so we've reduced it. These days we ask for a minimum of three months. Some people say two would be enough, but it takes weeks to learn the routines, and we like volunteers to be here long enough to be useful.
Three months is fine. I don't have any plans to move again.

Excellent. And one last thing. We provide a T-shirt and gloves, so you don't need to buy a uniform, but the cat house floors get wet when they're cleaned, so you'll need your own waterproof boots. Don't spend a lot on them, anything sturdy will do.
I've got an old pair of wellies. Would an overall be a good idea as well?
No, no need. Just the boots. Right, I'll put you down for the next induction session, and I'll email you the details this afternoon. Is the address on the poster still the best one for you?
Yes, please use that one. Thank you so much for your help, Tom.
My pleasure, Ellen. We'll see you soon. Bye for now.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A facilities manager tells staff about a new canteen and gym in the company building.
script: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming. I know it's early, so I'll try to keep this short. I'm here to tell you about the two projects that have taken up most of my year: the new staff canteen and the gym. Both of them open to everyone on the first of March.

Let me start with the canteen. Some of you will remember that the original plan was to put it in the basement, next to the old storeroom. That would have been the cheapest option, but the architects pointed out that nobody wants to eat lunch without a window, so we changed our minds. The canteen will now be on the top floor of the main building, with views over the river, and I think it's going to be the nicest place in the company to sit.

Why are we doing this at all? Well, you may remember the survey we sent round last spring. I expected people to tell me that the old canteen was too small, and a few of you did. But the real surprise was that sixty per cent of you said you left the site for lunch most days, usually because there was nowhere decent to eat here. That meant long lunch breaks and, frankly, a lot of money going to the sandwich shops on Bridge Street. We would rather you stayed with us, relaxed, and came back to your desks refreshed.

Now, the food. We've hired a head chef who used to run a restaurant in Wellington, and she is planning a new menu every week. She's very keen on freshness. We did consider growing vegetables on the roof, and we will have a few herb boxes up there, but that won't go very far. Instead, almost everything will come from farms within fifty kilometres of the city, and I think you'll taste the difference. Prices will be low. A main meal will cost 4 pounds 50, because the company is paying part of the cost.

Next, the gym. It's on the ground floor of the east wing, in the space that used to be the post room. We first proposed opening from 7 in the morning until 10 at night, but when we asked the early shift in the warehouse, they told us 7 would be too late for them. So the gym will open at 6 in the morning, and it will close at 10 at night as originally planned. That's 6 until 10, every day.

Before you can use any of the equipment, you have to complete an induction. It lasts about forty minutes, it covers safety and how to adjust the machines, and you can book it at reception from next Monday. A few people have asked me whether they need a letter from their doctor. You don't. And there's no joining fee either, so membership is free for all staff.

Let me now run through some of the other facilities, so that you know what to expect. First, the coffee bar by the main entrance. It opens at 7.30 every morning, so you can pick up a coffee before you start work, and it stays open all day.
Second, the yoga studio, which is next to the gym. It's a lovely room, but it's quite small, so classes are limited to 20 people. If a class is full, you can put your name on the waiting list.

Third, the terrace outside the canteen. I'd love to tell you that you can eat out there from the opening day, but the builders won't finish it until June, so for the first few months you'll just have to look at it through the windows.

Fourth, fitness assessments. Every new member of the gym is entitled to one assessment in their first month, and I'm happy to say that it's free. Normally it would cost 30 pounds, so do take advantage of it.

And finally, personal training. We have two trainers who will work with you one to one, but they are going to be very popular, so you'll need to book at least a week in advance. You can do that through the staff intranet.
Right, that's everything from me. If you have any questions, I'll be in the canteen after this meeting, and you're welcome to come and have a look at the plans on the wall. Thank you very much.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students discuss their case study of a family business.
script: Hi, Jack. Thanks for coming in early. I thought we should sort out the case study before Friday's tutorial.

Good idea. I've been thinking about it all week. I'm really glad we ended up with Ashdown Furniture. When the tutor first suggested a bakery, I wasn't keen, because we'd never have got an interview with the owners.
Right, and the bakery wasn't even a family business, as it turned out. But Ashdown works because of your cousin, doesn't it?
Yes, my cousin has worked in their showroom for six years, so he put me in touch with the owner, Daniel Ashdown. Without that connection, I doubt he'd have talked to us at all.
Well, whatever the reason, it's been a good choice. Do you remember what Dr Hale said about our proposal, though? I thought she was a bit harsh.

She said it was too broad. We tried to cover succession, marketing, finance and the history all in one report, and she told us to narrow it down. I think she's right. She wasn't complaining about the data or the research question, only the size of it.
So we're focusing on how the company has managed the change from one generation to the next. Which was the interesting bit anyway.

Exactly. So, for the background, the founder was Daniel's grandfather, Arthur. He actually started mending chairs in his garage in 1952, but the company wasn't officially registered until 1958, so I think we should start the timeline there, with the registration.
Fine by me. And the big decision came with Daniel himself, didn't it? I remember reading he thought about selling part of the business to an investor.

He considered it, yes, and so did his sister, but in the end they rejected the idea because they didn't want to lose control. What they did instead, and this is what I found really interesting, was to hire a manager from outside the family. That was a huge break with tradition, and it caused arguments for months.
Because the family had always run everything themselves.
Right. Anyway, what surprised you in the financial figures? You were going through the accounts last night.

I expected to find big debts, because they've invested so much in the new warehouse. But they're actually debt-free. What did surprise me was the salaries. The family members who run the company each pay themselves less than the senior staff they employ. I'd never have guessed that.
That's useful for our conclusion. It shows they put the business first.
Speaking of which, what do we recommend? I was wondering whether we should say that they need outside investment.

I'm not sure that's what the evidence shows. To me, the real lesson is that the company was lucky. Arthur's son got ill before there was any plan, and everything was done in a rush. So I'd conclude that succession planning should start much earlier in family firms.
Yes, I like that. It's more convincing than saying everyone should have the same shares, which is hard to prove anyway.
Good. So let's go through the presentation. Slide one is the history, with the timeline from 1958. Slide two is the family tree.
And slide three is the interview with the accountant. I've already recorded it, and she was very helpful about the salaries, so I'll play a short clip.
Great. Slide four, I thought we could have a photograph of the workshop. I took one when I visited, with the old machines in the background.
That would be better than a picture of the showroom. Then the graph. I've got the figures for the last five years, showing sales to online customers, which have tripled.
Tripled? That's a good one for slide five. And the last slide is the recommendation.
Okay. Now, about the handouts. Dr Hale said she wants a one-page summary for the audience, and we have to print them ourselves.
Then I'll do the handouts. I can print them in the library. And when is our slot? I thought it was Friday.
It was, but she's moved it to Thursday morning, so we have one day less than we thought. We should rehearse tomorrow afternoon.
Tomorrow's fine. I'll book a room. See you then.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about the part salt has played in human history.
script: Good afternoon. Today I'd like to talk about something so ordinary that we hardly notice it: salt. It sits on every dining table, yet for most of human history it was a precious commodity, and whole empires were built on controlling it.

Let me begin with why we need it. The human body cannot function without salt. It helps our nerves to send signals, and it helps to regulate the balance of water in our cells. We lose some every day through sweat, so we have to replace it, and that is why people have always gone to great lengths to find it.

For early hunter-gatherers, this wasn't a problem. The meat they ate contained enough salt for their needs. The difficulty began when people started farming. A diet based on cereals contains very little salt, so farming communities had to find it elsewhere, and that is when salt became a trade item. Some of the oldest known salt works, in China and in central Europe, date from around that time.

The second great use of salt was preservation. Before refrigeration, there was no way to keep food from rotting, except by drying it or by covering it in salt. Fish was the most important example. Salted fish could be carried on long journeys, and it fed armies, sailors and entire cities far from the sea. Without salt, the great voyages of exploration would have been very difficult indeed.

Now, let's look at the ancient world. The Romans, as you might expect, were extremely organised about salt. One of the main routes into Rome was known as the Via Salaria, which is spelled S-A-L-A-R-I-A, and it was used to carry salt from the coast to the city. You may also have heard that the word salary comes from salt, and that Roman soldiers were paid in it. Historians now doubt that last claim, but the word itself does come from the Latin for salt, and it shows how closely salt was linked to payment.

Elsewhere, salt was used as actual money. In parts of Ethiopia, until the twentieth century, travellers used blocks of rock salt for buying goods in the markets. A block was cut from a salt flat in the desert, carried by camel, and it was accepted as currency, so people literally carried their wealth with them.

In the Middle Ages, salt made some cities very rich. Venice is the best example. The Venetians didn't simply produce salt. They bought it from the Mediterranean coast and sold it on, and they controlled so much of the trade that other cities had to deal with them. The wealth they gained paid for the palaces that tourists visit today.

When a commodity is so important, governments want a share, and that brings me to taxation. The most notorious salt tax was the one in France, which was known as the gabelle, G-A-B-E-L-L-E. It existed in different forms for hundreds of years. What made it so hated was not only its size but the fact that each household was forced to buy a fixed amount of salt every year, whether they needed it or not. Smuggling was common, and punishments for smugglers were severe. The gabelle was one of the many grievances that fuelled the French Revolution, and it was abolished in 1790.

Salt taxes also affected the colonies. In India under British rule, there was a tax on salt that fell most heavily on the poor. In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi led a march to protest against it. He and his followers walked for 24 days, covering about 390 kilometres, until they reached the coast at Dandi, where he picked up a small lump of natural salt from the shore. It was an illegal act, and it became a powerful symbol of resistance, one that influenced the movement towards independence.

So what is the situation today? Refrigeration has removed the need to preserve food with salt, and salt is cheap and plentiful. In fact, you might be surprised to learn that most salt is no longer used in kitchens at all. The bulk of production goes to the chemical industry, where it is a raw material for making plastics, glass and a range of other products. Just a small fraction ends up on our dinner tables, and some of that is used in the winter to melt ice on roads.

To finish, I'd like you to think about how a substance that was once worth fighting over has become something we take for granted. In next week's lecture, I'll look at another commodity that shaped the world: sugar. Thank you.

passages.title: Concrete: the material that built the modern world
paras: A  Walk down almost any street in the world and you will be surrounded by concrete: in the pavement beneath your feet, in the foundations of the buildings, in the bridge that carries the traffic overhead. With the exception of water, it is the substance that human beings consume in the greatest quantity, and by some estimates the world now pours more than three tonnes of it each year for every person alive. Yet few of us give it a thought. Concrete is cheap, heavy, grey and unglamorous, and its very ordinariness has hidden a long and surprising history.

B  The basic idea is old. Builders in the eastern Mediterranean were mixing lime with sand and water more than four thousand years ago, but it was the Romans who turned the mixture into a system. Around the second century BC they discovered that adding volcanic ash from the region near Naples made the mortar set even when submerged, which allowed them to build harbours directly into the sea. Their engineers also learned to lighten large structures by placing heavy stone in the lower layers of a wall and pumice, a light volcanic rock, in the upper ones. The dome of the Pantheon in Rome, completed in the second century AD, was cast in this way. It contains no steel at all, and it remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

C  After the Roman Empire declined, much of this knowledge was lost. For roughly a thousand years, European builders relied mainly on stone, brick and timber, and the recipe for a truly durable cement had to be found again. The breakthrough came in 1824, when an English bricklayer named Joseph Aspdin took out a patent for a powder made by heating limestone and clay at a high temperature and grinding the result. He called it Portland cement because, once set, it resembled a well-known building stone quarried on the Dorset coast. Modern cement is a refined descendant of Aspdin's invention, and concrete is simply cement mixed with water and an aggregate such as sand or gravel. The cement acts as a glue, and the aggregate gives the finished material its bulk.

D  Concrete has one great weakness. It is very strong when squeezed but weak when stretched, so a long beam of it will crack under its own weight. The solution, developed in France and Germany in the later nineteenth century, was to bury steel bars in the concrete as it set. Steel resists stretching, concrete resists squeezing, and the two change size at almost the same rate when the temperature rises or falls, a lucky coincidence on which the whole technique depends. Reinforced concrete made it possible to build tall frames, wide bridges and thin curved roofs that would have been impossible in stone. Early in the twentieth century, architects began to treat it not merely as a hidden structure but as a visible material in its own right, with a texture and character of its own.

E  The middle decades of the century were the age of concrete's greatest popularity and, in the view of many critics, of its greatest misuse. Cities damaged by war needed homes quickly, and concrete panels could be made in factories and bolted together on site by workers with little training. Housing estates, car parks and shopping centres of this kind spread across Europe and Asia. Many were badly maintained and became deeply unpopular, and the architectural style known as Brutalism, named after the French phrase for raw concrete, still divides opinion today. Yet attitudes are changing. Some of the buildings once regarded as eyesores are now protected by law, and a younger generation of visitors has discovered a stark beauty in their heavy shapes.

F  A more serious difficulty is environmental. Making cement requires heating limestone to around 1,450 degrees Celsius, which consumes huge amounts of energy, and the chemical reaction that turns limestone into cement releases carbon dioxide of its own. As a result, cement manufacture is responsible for around eight per cent of the world's carbon emissions, a larger share than aviation. Because demand is growing fastest in countries that are still building their cities and roads, the problem is likely to get worse before it gets better.

G  Researchers are therefore searching for alternatives. Some replace a portion of the cement with industrial waste, such as the ash left by coal-fired power stations. Others inject carbon dioxide into the mixture while it hardens, so that the gas becomes permanently trapped in the finished material. Another approach is self-healing concrete, which contains dormant bacteria that wake when water enters a crack and produce limestone to seal it, thereby extending the life of a structure and reducing the need for repairs. Whether any of these ideas will be adopted on a large scale depends largely on cost, since the very cheapness that made concrete so successful is also what makes it so difficult to replace.

passages.title: Living light
paras: A  Below about a thousand metres, no sunlight reaches the ocean, and for centuries naturalists assumed that the deep sea was a place of permanent darkness. They were wrong. When researchers began to explore the open ocean with submersibles and cameras, they found that it was alive with flashes, glows and drifting clouds of light. Some surveys suggest that around three-quarters of the animals living in open water can produce light themselves, a phenomenon known as bioluminescence. It is also found on land, in fireflies, glow-worms and certain fungi, but the sea is where it is most common. In the dark waters of the deep, the ability to make light is not an exotic exception. It is the normal state of affairs.

B  The chemistry is surprisingly simple. A light-emitting molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, a reaction speeded up by an enzyme called luciferase, and the energy released emerges as light. Unlike the glow of a lamp, almost none of that energy is lost as heat, which is why bioluminescence is sometimes described as cold light. The process has evolved on many separate occasions. Biologists believe that it has arisen independently at least forty times, in groups as different as bacteria, jellyfish, beetles and fish, and the luciferins used by different groups are often chemically unrelated. This repeated invention suggests that being able to make light offers an enormous advantage.

C  For many animals the advantage is defence. Some squid and shrimp release a glowing cloud when attacked, in the same way that an octopus releases ink, leaving the predator confused while the prey escapes. Others use light for camouflage. In deep water, a predator looking upwards sees the faint glow of the surface, and any animal above it appears as a dark shape against that light. The Hawaiian bobtail squid solves this problem by shining light from its underside, matching the brightness of the moonlit water above, so that its shadow all but disappears. Tiny single-celled organisms called dinoflagellates have a more unusual strategy. They flash when they are disturbed by a small predator, and this may act as a kind of burglar alarm, because the flash attracts larger animals that are likely to eat the attacker.

D  Light can also be used to attract. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth, and small fish that come to investigate are swallowed. On land, fireflies use their flashes to find mates. Males fly over the grass, producing a pattern of flashes that is different for every species, and females answer from the ground with their own signal. The system is not entirely honest, however. Females of one genus have learned to imitate the replies of other species, and when a male of the wrong species arrives, expecting a mate, he is eaten instead.

E  Many luminous animals do not make light on their own. Instead they keep colonies of glowing bacteria in special organs. The bobtail squid is the best-studied example. Shortly after hatching, a young squid collects a particular species of bacterium from the seawater and houses it in a pouch beneath its body. The bacteria receive food and shelter, and the squid receives a built-in lamp. Each dawn, the squid expels about ninety per cent of its bacteria into the sea and keeps the rest, which multiply during the day, so that by nightfall the lamp is bright once again. Other partnerships, including those of certain fish, work in a similar way.

F  Humans have found uses for these living lights. The gene for firefly luciferase can be inserted into laboratory cells, which then glow, allowing researchers to follow the spread of cancer cells inside living mice without having to operate on them. In another application, bacteria that glow in the presence of certain toxins are used to test samples of drinking water; a faint glow signals contamination. More speculative ideas have also been put forward. Some designers have proposed that trees could be engineered to glow and so replace street lamps, saving electricity. Most scientists regard this as unrealistic, since the light produced by even the brightest known organisms is far too weak for reading or walking at night.

G  Despite decades of research, bioluminescence still holds mysteries. For a long time, no one knew why some fungi on the forest floor give off a steady green light at night. In an experiment in Brazil, researchers placed sticky traps next to artificial fungi, some of which were lit by small green lights while others were left dark. The glowing models attracted far more insects, which suggests that the fungi use light to lure animals that will carry their spores to new places. Experiments of this kind show how much remains to be learned, even about creatures that have been glowing quietly in the dark for millions of years.

passages.title: Counting what counts
paras: A  Few numbers have shaped modern politics as much as gross domestic product, the total value of everything produced within a country in a year. It was developed in the 1930s by the economist Simon Kuznets, who had been asked by the American government to measure the effects of the Depression. Yet Kuznets himself was uneasy about how his invention might be used. He warned that the welfare of a nation could scarcely be inferred from a measure of its income, and he urged policy makers to consider what kind of growth they were pursuing, and at what cost. His caution was largely ignored. Within a few decades, GDP had become the standard way of judging whether a country was succeeding, and a rise or fall of a single percentage point could decide an election.

B  The trouble is that GDP counts activity, not benefit. It adds up money spent, without asking whether that spending made anyone better off. An oil spill is, in a narrow accounting sense, good news: the money spent on clean-up crews, equipment and lawyers all appears in the figures as additional output. A bitter divorce raises GDP, and so does a crime wave that sends people to buy alarms and locks. Meanwhile, much of what makes life worth living does not appear at all. The unpaid work of caring for children and elderly relatives, which has been estimated to be worth a very large share of the economy in many countries, is left out because no money changes hands. A society could become poorer in any meaningful sense while its GDP rose, and it is surprising how rarely this paradox is discussed in public.

C  A second problem is that GDP is an average, and averages conceal. Imagine two countries with identical GDP per person. In the first, income is spread fairly evenly. In the second, a small group captures most of the gains and the majority has seen no improvement in a generation. The headline figures are the same, but the lives of the people involved are very different. As economists have studied inequality more closely, it has become clear that the average citizen's experience may differ greatly from what the national total implies, and that rising GDP may be accompanied by falling living standards for many families.

D  A third criticism concerns the environment. When a forest is felled and sold, the sale adds to GDP, but the loss of the standing forest, with its ability to store carbon and absorb floodwater, appears in no column. A country may therefore grow richer on paper by consuming the resources on which its future prosperity depends, a practice that any business owner would recognise as running down the capital. In response, some economists have proposed national accounts based on the idea of natural capital, in which forests, soils and fisheries are treated as assets that can gain or lose value from year to year. Progress has been slow, but a number of governments have begun to publish such figures alongside the traditional ones.

E  None of this means that GDP is useless, and critics who treat it as worthless make a serious error. Richer countries, on average, have longer life expectancy, lower infant mortality and higher levels of literacy than poorer ones, and these benefits are not accidental. They are paid for out of growth. To tell a country where most people lack clean water and basic medical care that economic expansion does not matter would be both foolish and cruel. The real task is not to abandon the measure but to stop treating it as the whole story, especially in societies that have long passed the point where more output translates into more well-being.

F  Several alternatives have been proposed. The Human Development Index combines income with health and education. Surveys of happiness, now carried out regularly in many countries, ask people directly how satisfied they are with their lives. Bhutan went further in the 1970s, declaring that it would pursue Gross National Happiness rather than Gross National Product, although how far this has changed daily life in that country is hard to judge. These efforts are valuable, but I am sceptical that any single replacement can succeed. Every composite index involves choices about what to include and how to weigh one factor against another, and those choices are not technical decisions. They are value judgements, which a single number conceals rather than resolves.

G  A more realistic course is to give up the search for one number altogether and present a dashboard of indicators: income, health, education, the state of the environment, the distribution of wealth and the amount of time people spend at work or with their families. GDP would remain on the dashboard, but only as one gauge among many. The obstacle is political. A single, easily compared figure is irresistible to governments, because it allows them to claim success or deny failure in a single sentence. The news media, which report the quarterly figure as though it were a verdict on the nation, share the blame. Until journalists and voters demand a richer picture, politicians have little reason to offer one.

H  The aim, in the end, is modest. A measure of progress should tell us whether life is improving for the people living it, and the numbers we use should be chosen with that question in mind. We have spent nearly a century counting what is easy to count. It is time to begin counting what matters.
